intro: Almost every street trick starts with one move: the ollie, a jump in which the board rises with the skater and nothing holds it but the feet. Alan 'Ollie' Gelfand popped it on ramps and bowls in the late 1970s, and Rodney Mullen brought it to flat ground in the early 1980s. Flip tricks such as the kickflip and heelflip grew out of that flat-ground ollie. This unit teaches the ollie and three tricks built on it, step by step.

Each trick is taught the same careful way. Gear comes first: a helmet that fits and is buckled, wrist guards and pads, and flat shoes. Practice starts standing still on grass or carpet, then moves to rolling slowly on smooth, flat ground away from cars. Directions say front foot and back foot, so they work for regular and goofy skaters alike. Common problems come with their fixes.

Along the way you will see the science under the board. The tail and back wheels make a lever. The ground pushes back when the tail strikes it. Grip tape friction pulls the board up. Bent knees soften a landing, and a flick at the edge of the deck makes a torque that rolls the board around its long axis. By the end you will be able to explain each step of a trick and the physics behind it.
bigQuestion: How do your feet, your timing and a few laws of physics work together to make a skateboard jump, spin and flip?

timeline.t: Buckle a helmet that fits and put on wrist guards, pads and flat shoes
Set the board on grass: back foot on the tail, front foot behind the front bolts
Crouch and practice the pop until the tail clacks and bounces
Add the front-foot slide, the jump and the knee lift
Level the board and land with both feet over the bolts, knees bent
Try small rolling ollies at walking speed on smooth, flat ground
Learn the pop shove-it: scoop the tail for a 180 degree flat spin
Learn the kickflip flick off the toe-side corner of the nose, on grass first
Learn the heelflip flick off the heel-side corner of the nose
Catch each flip with both feet over the bolts, then try it rolling slowly

words.d: a jump in which the skater pops the tail and the board rises with the feet, with no hands
snapping the tail hard against the ground so the board bounces up
a stiff bar that turns around a fixed point; in the ollie, the board turns around the back wheels
a force that resists one surface sliding across another, such as a shoe on grip tape
the way an object keeps moving the same way unless a force changes it
the screw heads on top of the deck that show where the trucks are; feet land over them
a trick in which the board spins 180 degrees flat under the skater
an ollie in which the front foot flicks off the toe-side edge of the nose so the board rolls once
an ollie in which the front heel flicks off the heel-side edge of the nose so the board rolls once
an imaginary line that an object turns around; a board has a long, a short and a vertical axis
a turning push; torque equals force times the distance from the axis
to stop a turning board with the feet and land on it

test.q: What is the correct order of the ollie?
choices: Pop, crouch, slide, level, jump, land
Crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land
Slide, pop, crouch, jump, land, level
Crouch, slide, pop, land, level, jump
test.why: Crouch, pop the tail, slide the front foot, jump, level the board, then land.

test.q: Which foot pops the tail in an ollie?
choices: Neither; the hands lift the board
test.why: The ball of the back foot snaps the tail down; the front foot slides toward the nose.

test.q: In an ollie, the back wheels act as what?
test.why: The board turns around the back wheels like a lever, so the nose swings up when the tail goes down.

test.q: Who brought the ollie to flat ground in the early 1980s?
test.why: Alan Gelfand did the first ollies on transition in the late 1970s; Rodney Mullen did them on flat ground.

test.q: What pulls the board upward as the front foot slides?
choices: Friction between the shoe and the grip tape
test.why: Rough grip tape creates friction, so the board follows the dragging shoe up.

test.q: About how long does a 0.30 m ollie stay in the air?
A 50 kg rider landing at 2.4 m/s stops in 0.10 s. What is the stopping force?
test.why: Deceleration = 2.4 ÷ 0.10 = 24 m/s², and F = ma = 50 × 24 = 1,200 N.

test.q: Why should you land an ollie with both feet over the bolts?
choices: The bolts are over the trucks, so the board stays balanced and strong
The bolts are the softest part
test.why: The trucks are the strongest part of the board, and landing over both keeps it balanced and rolling straight.

test.q: In a pop shove-it, the board spins around which axis?
test.why: The board spins flat like a plate, around a line straight up and down through the deck.

test.q: Which foot does most of the work in a backside pop shove-it?
choices: The front foot, flicking the nose
The back foot, popping and scooping the tail behind you
test.why: The back foot pops and scoops; the front foot just lifts out of the way.

test.q: How does a kickflip flick differ from a heelflip flick?
choices: The kickflip uses the heel; the heelflip uses the side of the foot
The kickflip uses the back foot
The kickflip flicks off the toe-side edge; the heelflip off the heel-side edge
test.why: The pushes land on opposite edges, so the two boards roll in opposite directions.

test.q: A 20 N flick lands 0.05 m from the long axis. What is the torque?
Why does a board roll more easily around its long axis than around its vertical axis?
choices: Its mass sits close to the long axis, so its rotational inertia there is smaller
The long axis has less gravity
test.why: A narrow deck keeps its mass near the long axis; the nose and tail sit far from the vertical axis.

test.q: What is a good first step for learning a kickflip?
choices: Flick the board on grass without popping, holding a fence
test.why: The flick alone on grass is the smallest step; pops, catches and rolling come later.

test.q: During a rolling ollie, you feel scared and start leaning back. What should you do?
choices: Go back a step: roll slower or practice pops standing still
test.why: Fear is a normal signal; a smaller step builds confidence, and leaning back sends the board out in front of you.

write.prompt: Explain how to do an ollie, step by step, to a friend who has never tried one. Use front foot and back foot. Then explain the physics of two steps: the pop (the lever and the ground pushing back) and the landing (why bent knees lower the force). Include one calculation.
tips: Start with gear and a safe, flat practice spot.
Name each step in order: crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land.
Say what each foot does and what it should feel like.
Show every step of your calculation, with units.
End with one common problem and its fix.

title: Ollies and Flip Tricks

chapters.title: The Ollie Step by Step
chapters.bigQuestion: How do a few quick moves, done in the right order, lift a skateboard off flat ground and bring it back under your feet?

story.title: The Carpet in the Garage
story.kicker: Hundreds of tries on a carpet come before the first rolling ollie.
paragraphs: Jordan dragged an old piece of carpet into the garage on the first cold Saturday of fall. The skateboard went on top of it, and its wheels sank into the soft pile. Jordan buckled a helmet, pulled on wrist guards and stood with the back foot on the tail. The board did not roll an inch. That was the point.

The first pops were slow and heavy. The nose rose a little and then thumped back down. Jordan's front foot stayed planted like a brick. A cousin who skated watched for a minute and gave one tip: snap the tail fast, then drag the front shoe up toward the nose. Jordan tried again. The clack of the tail was sharper this time.

By December, a sheet of paper was taped to the garage wall. Each mark on it stood for a clean try, with all four wheels off the carpet and both feet landing over the bolts. The marks crowded into rows of five. Some days the count went up by twenty. Some days it went up by two. The side of Jordan's front shoe wore pale and rough.

In early spring Jordan carried the board to a dry, empty basketball court. Push, roll slowly, set the feet. Crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land. The board rose a few centimeters and came down under both feet, still rolling. It was a small ollie. It counted. Every mark on that garage wall had been part of it.
story.think: Why might Jordan have practiced on carpet for months before trying an ollie while rolling?

lessons.title: Gear for Ollie Practice
lessons.mainIdea: A buckled helmet that fits, wrist guards, pads and flat shoes let you practice the ollie and fall without serious harm.
reading: Learning the ollie means falling many times, so gear comes before the first try. A *helmet* should sit level on your head, about two finger-widths above your eyebrows. Buckle the chin strap so only one or two fingers fit under it. Shake your head side to side. A helmet that fits stays put and does not slide back to show your forehead.

*Wrist guards* matter because wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries. When people fall, they reach out with their hands. A wrist guard has a stiff splint that spreads the shock along the forearm. Knee pads and elbow pads let you slide on hard plastic caps instead of skin. Pads that fit snugly stay in place when you land on them.

Shoes matter more for the ollie than for most first tricks. Choose flat shoes with a grippy rubber sole and no raised heel. Running shoes with thick, rounded soles make it hard to feel the board. The ollie rubs the side of the front shoe across rough grip tape, so a sturdy shoe lasts longer. Many skaters see a worn patch on that side of the front shoe after a few weeks.

Gear works best with a plan for falling. If you feel a fall coming, crouch low so you have less distance to drop. Try to roll onto your shoulder or slide on your knee pads. Keep your arms bent and loose. Locked, straight arms send the whole shock into your wrists and elbows.

words.d: a hard shell with foam inside that protects the head; it should fit snugly and be buckled
gloves with a stiff splint that protect the wrists when a skater falls onto the hands

look.title: The Mirror Check
look.text: Stand in front of a mirror with your helmet on. The front edge sits low on your forehead, about two fingers above your eyebrows. The side straps make a V just under each ear. The chin strap is buckled and snug. Now push the front of the helmet up with your palm. If it slides back and shows your whole forehead, the straps need tightening.
look.prompt: Do the push test with your own helmet. What, if anything, did you need to adjust?

check.q: Why do skaters learning the ollie wear wrist guards?
choices: Wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries
Wrist guards make the board pop higher
Wrist guards keep the hands warm
Wrist guards are needed only in contests
check.why: People reach out with their hands when they fall, and wrist injuries are among the most common in skateboarding. The splint in a wrist guard spreads the shock.

check.q: How should a well-fitted helmet sit?
choices: Tipped back so the forehead shows
Level, about two finger-widths above the eyebrows, with the strap buckled
Loose, so it can turn easily
Unbuckled, so it comes off fast in a fall
check.why: A helmet protects only when it sits level and low on the forehead and the strap is buckled snugly.

check.q: Which is the safest way to fall?
choices: Catch yourself with straight, locked arms
Crouch low and roll or slide on your knee pads
Hold on to the board with both hands
check.why: Crouching lowers the fall, and rolling or sliding spreads the shock. Locked arms send the shock into the wrists and elbows.

lessons.title: A Good Place to Practice
lessons.mainIdea: Practice on a flat, smooth, dry surface away from cars, and start on grass or carpet, where the wheels cannot roll.
reading: The best ollie spot is plain and boring. It is *flat ground*: level, smooth and dry. A quiet basketball court, an empty lot closed to cars, or the flat section of a *skatepark* all work. Wet pavement can make the wheels slip out without warning. Cracks and sand can grab a wheel. Walk the spot first and kick away pebbles, because one small stone can stop a wheel and throw you forward.

Stay far from streets and driveways. A board that shoots out from under you can roll into traffic, and you might chase it without looking. Pick a spot where a loose board stops on grass or against a wall, not in a road. Skateparks are built for practice like this, and many post their own gear rules at the gate.

Your very first ollie practice does not need pavement at all. On thick grass or carpet, the wheels sink in and cannot roll. That lets you learn the motion while the board stays right under you. The board will pop lower on a soft surface, and that is fine. The goal on grass is to learn the order of the moves, not to jump high.

words.d: a level, smooth surface with no ramps, used for practicing tricks such as the ollie
a place built for skateboarding, with ramps, ledges and flat areas

look.title: Two Spots Side by Side
look.text: Spot A is a smooth school blacktop on a dry Saturday, with a fence on one side and grass on the other. Spot B is a sloped driveway that ends at a street, with wet leaves and a few pebbles on it. Picture a board shooting out from under a skater at each spot. At Spot A it rolls into the grass and stops. At Spot B it rolls downhill toward the street.
look.prompt: List three things that make Spot A the safer choice. What would you still check before practicing there?

check.q: Why is a sloped driveway that ends at a street a poor place to practice ollies?
choices: A loose board can roll downhill into the street
check.why: A board that shoots out can roll into traffic. A good spot lets a loose board stop on grass or against a wall.

check.q: Why do learners often start the ollie on grass or carpet?
choices: The wheels sink in and cannot roll, so the board stays under them
check.why: On a soft surface the wheels cannot roll, so a learner can work on the order of the moves while the board stays still.

check.q: What should you do before practicing on a new spot?
choices: Walk it and kick away pebbles and sand
Wet the ground so it grips better
Practice close to the street so friends can see
Lean the board against a parked car
check.why: One small stone can stop a wheel and throw you forward, so clearing the spot first prevents falls.

lessons.title: Where Your Feet Go
lessons.mainIdea: Put the ball of your back foot on the tail and your front foot just behind the front bolts, across the board.
reading: Every ollie starts with the feet in the right place. Look at the top of the deck. Near each end you will see four *bolts*, the screw heads that hold the trucks on. The *tail* is the kicked-up end behind the back bolts. The *nose* is the kicked-up end in front of the front bolts.

Your back foot goes on the tail. Put the ball of your foot, the padded part just behind the toes, near the middle of the tail. Your heel can hang slightly off the edge. Do not stand on the tail with only your toes. The ball of the foot lets you snap down hard and then lift off quickly.

Your front foot goes just behind the front bolts, pointing across the board or angled slightly toward the nose. Leave a gap of about a hand's width behind the bolts, so the foot has room to slide forward. If you ride with your left foot forward, you are *regular*. Right foot forward is *goofy*. Both are normal, which is why skaters say front foot and back foot instead of left and right.

Check your stance by standing on the board on grass. Your feet should be about shoulder-width apart, with your weight even between them. If the nose lifts while you stand still, your back foot is carrying too much weight.

words.d: the screw heads on top of the deck that hold the trucks on; there are four near each end
the kicked-up end of the board behind the back bolts
the kicked-up end of the board in front of the front bolts
riding with the left foot forward
riding with the right foot forward

look.title: A Bird's-Eye View of the Stance
look.text: Look down at a skater standing ready for an ollie. The back foot sits on the tail, the ball of the foot near the middle and the heel hanging just off the edge. The front foot lies across the board a hand's width behind the front bolts. The feet are about as far apart as the shoulders. The nose and tail both rest flat on the ground.
look.prompt: Stand on a board on grass in this stance. Where does your weight feel heaviest, and what would you change to make it even?

check.q: Where does the back foot go for an ollie?
choices: The ball of the foot near the middle of the tail
In the middle of the deck
check.why: The ball of the back foot on the tail lets the skater snap the tail down hard and lift off quickly.

check.q: Where does the front foot start?
choices: Just behind the front bolts, across the board
Off the board, on the ground
check.why: The front foot starts a hand's width behind the front bolts so it has room to slide toward the nose.

check.q: A skater rides with the right foot forward. What is that stance called?
check.why: Right foot forward is goofy and left foot forward is regular. Both are normal stances.

lessons.title: Crouch to Load Your Legs
lessons.mainIdea: Bending your knees low before the pop gives your legs a longer push, so you can jump higher.
reading: Before you pop, you *crouch*. Bend your knees and lower your hips as if you were about to sit in a chair. Keep your back fairly straight and your head up. Your shoulders should line up with the board, pointing toward the nose and the tail. A twisted upper body tends to twist the board too.

The crouch is where the jump's energy starts. A jump is a push against the ground. The lower you bend, the longer your legs can push before your feet leave the board. A longer push sends your body higher. Nobody can jump high from straight legs, and the same is true on a skateboard.

Do not crouch so low that you lose your balance. A good crouch feels springy, not stuck. Your weight stays over the middle of the board, between your feet. If the nose lifts while you crouch, you are leaning back. Move your hips forward until the board sits flat again. Keeping a steady *stance* in the crouch makes every later step easier.

words.d: to bend the knees and lower the body to get ready for a jump
the way a skater stands on the board, including where each foot goes

look.title: A Spring Being Squeezed
look.text: Picture a metal spring standing on a table. Press it halfway down with your hand, then let go, and it jumps a little. Press it all the way down, then let go, and it jumps much higher. Your legs work in a similar way. A deeper crouch lets them push for longer before your feet leave the board.
look.prompt: Try two small jumps on the ground, one from a shallow bend and one from a deep crouch. Which went higher, and why?

check.q: Why do skaters crouch before popping an ollie?
choices: Bending gives the legs a longer push, so the jump goes higher
It keeps the wheels from turning
check.why: The lower you bend, the longer your legs can push against the board, and a longer push sends your body higher.

check.q: Where should your weight be during the crouch?
choices: Over the middle of the board, between your feet
check.why: Weight over the middle keeps the board flat and balanced until the pop.

check.q: While you crouch, the nose lifts off the ground. What does that tell you?
choices: You are leaning back and should move your hips forward
Your front foot is too far back
check.why: A nose that lifts in the crouch means too much weight is behind you, on the tail.

lessons.title: Snap the Tail
lessons.mainIdea: The back foot strikes the tail down hard and fast, the ground pushes back, and the board tips nose-up and rises.
reading: The *pop* is the sound and the move that start every ollie. From the crouch, your back foot snaps the tail down hard and fast so it strikes the ground. You hear a sharp clack. Right after the snap, you lift off the back foot and start to jump. The snap and the jump happen almost together, like one motion.

Here is the science. The board acts as a *lever*, a stiff bar that turns around a point. The back wheels are the *pivot*, the point it turns around. When the tail goes down, the nose swings up. When the tail hits the ground, the ground pushes back up on it. This is Newton's third law: when you push on something, it pushes back on you with an equal force. That push bounces the tail up and lifts the whole board into the air.

A quick snap works better than a slow push. A slow push only tips the board up like a seesaw, and it stays on the ground. A fast snap makes the tail hit the ground and rebound. Think popping, not pressing. If the board barely leaves the ground, snap faster and make sure the ball of your foot strikes the tail.

The trick is named for Alan 'Ollie' Gelfand. In the late 1970s he popped his board into the air without grabbing it while riding the curved walls of ramps and bowls. Skaters began calling the move the ollie. In the early 1980s Rodney Mullen showed it could be done on flat ground. His flat-ground ollie is the version you are learning now.

words.d: snapping the tail hard against the ground so the board bounces up
a stiff bar that turns around a fixed point; pushing one end down lifts the other end
the point a lever turns around; in the ollie, the back wheels

look.title: Newton's Third Law
look.text: To every action there is always opposed an equal reaction: or the mutual actions of two bodies upon each other are always equal, and directed to contrary parts.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia (1687), Law III, in Andrew Motte's English translation (1729)
look.prompt: In the ollie, what is the action and what is the reaction? Name the two bodies that push on each other.

check.q: In the ollie, what acts as the pivot of the lever?
check.why: The board turns around the back wheels: when the tail goes down, the nose swings up.

check.q: What does Newton's third law explain about the pop?
choices: The ground pushes back up on the tail when the tail strikes it
Grip tape keeps the shoe from sliding
check.why: When the tail pushes on the ground, the ground pushes back with an equal force, which bounces the board up.

check.q: Who is the ollie named after?
check.why: Alan 'Ollie' Gelfand popped no-hands airs on ramps and bowls in the late 1970s. Rodney Mullen later took the ollie to flat ground.

lessons.title: Slide the Front Foot Up
lessons.mainIdea: Right after the pop, the front foot drags up the grip tape toward the nose, pulling the board higher.
reading: Right after the pop, your front foot slides forward toward the nose. Roll your front ankle a little so the outside edge of the shoe, the little-toe side, brushes up the board. The foot moves up and forward at the same time. Picture dragging your shoe up a steep hill.

*Grip tape* is the sandpaper-like sheet stuck to the top of the deck. Its rough surface creates a lot of *friction*, a force that resists two surfaces sliding across each other. As your shoe drags upward, friction pulls the board up with it. On a smooth deck with no grip tape, the shoe would slip and the board would drop. That drag is also why the front shoe wears on its side.

Timing matters. Start the slide as soon as the tail pops, not before. If you slide too early, the nose never comes up. If you slide too late, the board rises and then falls back toward the tail. Slide until your front foot reaches the start of the nose's curve. Then get ready to push the nose down.

words.d: a rough, sandpaper-like sheet on top of the deck that keeps shoes from slipping
a force that resists one surface sliding across another

look.title: The Slide in Slow Motion
look.text: Watch an ollie at quarter speed from the side. The tail strikes the ground. The nose tilts up. The front shoe rolls onto its outside edge and creeps up the grip tape toward the nose, and the board rises right along with it, as if the shoe were pulling it on a string. When the shoe reaches the curve of the nose, the board is at its highest.
look.prompt: Stand on grass and practice only the front-foot slide, slowly. What part of your shoe touches the grip tape?

check.q: Which part of the front shoe brushes up the grip tape?
choices: The outside edge, on the little-toe side
The tip of the big toe only
check.why: Rolling the ankle a little lets the outside edge of the shoe drag up the grip tape.

check.q: What force lets the front foot pull the board upward?
choices: Friction between the shoe and the grip tape
check.why: Rough grip tape creates friction, so the board moves up along with the dragging shoe.

check.q: What happens if the front foot slides too early, before the pop?
choices: The board goes higher than usual
check.why: The slide must follow the pop. Sliding first keeps weight on the front of the board, so the nose stays down.

lessons.title: Jump and Pull Your Knees Up
lessons.mainIdea: After the pop, jump straight up and lift both knees toward your chest so the board has room to rise.
reading: The board can only rise as high as your feet let it. So after the pop, jump straight up and pull your knees toward your chest. The back knee comes up quickly so the tail can rise. The front knee comes up as the front foot slides. Your feet stay light on the board without stomping on it.

Jump up, not forward. When you are rolling, you and the board both move forward. Your body keeps that forward motion through the air on its own. This is *inertia*, the way a moving object keeps moving the same way unless a force changes it. If you also jump forward, you land in front of the board.

While you are in the air, gravity pulls you down the whole time. Your *center of mass*, the balance point of your body, rises and then falls in a smooth arch. Each move must happen fast, because an ollie lasts only a fraction of a second.

You can work out how long. For an ollie of height h, time in the air = 2 × √(2h ÷ g), with g = 9.8 m/s². For a 0.30 m ollie: 2 × 0.30 = 0.60. Then 0.60 ÷ 9.8 ≈ 0.061. The square root of 0.061 is about 0.247. Finally 2 × 0.247 ≈ 0.49 seconds, about half a second.

words.d: the way an object keeps moving the same way, or stays still, unless a force changes it
the balance point of a body or object, where its mass acts as if it were gathered

look.title: Time in the Air
look.cite: Worked example with g = 9.8 m/s²: time = 2 × √(2h ÷ g)
look.prompt: How much longer is a 0.30 m ollie in the air than a 0.10 m ollie? Show the subtraction.

check.q: Why should you pull your knees up after the pop?
choices: To give the board room to rise
To stop the board from rolling
To push the nose into the ground
check.why: The board can rise only as high as your feet let it, so lifting the knees makes room.

check.q: While rolling, why should you jump straight up instead of forward?
choices: Jumping up makes the wheels spin faster
Your body's inertia already carries you forward with the board
The board stops when you jump
check.why: Inertia keeps your forward motion going in the air. Jumping forward as well puts you ahead of the board.

check.q: About how long is a 0.30 m ollie in the air?
check.why: 2 × √(2 × 0.30 ÷ 9.8) ≈ 2 × 0.247 ≈ 0.49 seconds, about half a second.

lessons.title: Level the Board
lessons.mainIdea: At the top of the jump, the front foot pushes the nose down while the back knee lifts, so the board flattens out.
reading: After the slide, the board is tilted with the nose high. To *level* it, press your front foot gently forward and down on the nose. At the same time, keep lifting your back knee so the tail can rise. The board flattens out under you like a table top. The best ollies level out right at the top of the jump.

Leveling is another lever action. The front foot pushes down near the nose, in front of the front wheels. The back foot rises and gets out of the way. The board turns around its middle until it is flat. If the front foot pushes too hard, the nose dips and the board lands nose first.

Picture the board's path from the side. First the tail goes down and the nose goes up, a steep *tilt*. Then the whole board rises. Then it flattens. Then it falls with you. That order, crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land, is the whole ollie.

words.d: to make the board flat in the air by pushing the nose down and lifting the back knee
a slant, when one end of the board is higher than the other

look.title: Four Snapshots From the Side
look.text: Snapshot 1: the tail touches the ground and the nose points up at the sky. Snapshot 2: the board is off the ground and still tilted, with the front shoe near the nose. Snapshot 3: the board is flat at the top of the jump, both knees high. Snapshot 4: the board is coming down flat, with both feet over the bolts.
look.prompt: Act out the four snapshots slowly on grass. In which snapshot does the front foot push down?

check.q: How does the front foot level the board?
choices: It lifts straight up off the board
It presses forward and down on the nose
It pushes down on the tail
check.why: Pressing the nose down while the back knee lifts turns the board flat.

check.q: What happens if the front foot pushes the nose down too hard?
choices: The board lands on the tail
check.why: Too much push dips the nose below level, so the nose touches down first.

check.q: Which list shows the ollie in the right order?
choices: Pop, crouch, level, slide, jump, land
Slide, pop, crouch, land, jump, level
Crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land
Jump, crouch, land, pop, slide, level
check.why: You crouch, pop the tail, slide the front foot, jump, level the board, then land.

lessons.title: Land Over the Bolts
lessons.mainIdea: Land with both feet over the bolts and bend your knees, which spreads the landing over more time and lowers the force.
reading: Aim to land with both feet over the bolts. The bolts sit above the trucks, the strongest part of the board. Landing on the middle of the deck can crack it. Landing on the tail can make the board shoot out. Landing over both trucks keeps the board balanced and the wheels rolling straight.

Bend your knees as you land. Your legs work like *shock absorbers*, the springy parts that soften bumps in a car. When you land stiff-legged, your body stops in a very short time. When you bend, it stops over a longer time. Stopping the same motion over a longer time takes less force, so your knees, ankles and board feel less of a jolt.

Here is a worked example. A 50 kg rider drops 0.30 m from the top of an ollie. Speed at landing is about √(2 × 9.8 × 0.30) = √5.88 ≈ 2.4 m/s. Stopping in 0.05 s with stiff legs, the *deceleration* is 2.4 ÷ 0.05 = 48 m/s². The force is F = ma = 50 × 48 = 2,400 N. Bending to stop in 0.20 s gives 2.4 ÷ 0.20 = 12 m/s², and 50 × 12 = 600 N. That is one quarter of the force, on top of the rider's weight.

After you land, stay low for a moment and roll away. Keep your shoulders over the board until it feels steady. Rolling away cleanly is part of the trick. If the board wobbles as it rolls away, check where your feet landed. Feet near the middle of the deck make the board feel tippy, so aim for the bolts next time.

words.d: springy parts that soften a bump by spreading it over more time; bent knees act like them
slowing down; how much speed is lost each second, in meters per second per second
the SI unit of force, written N; a small apple of about 100 g weighs about 1 N

look.title: Stopping Time and Landing Force
look.cite: Worked example: 50 kg rider landing at 2.4 m/s; force = mass × (speed ÷ stopping time), not counting body weight
look.prompt: What happens to the force each time the stopping time doubles? Check two rows to prove it.

check.q: Where should your feet be when you land an ollie?
choices: Both in the middle of the deck
check.why: The bolts sit over the trucks, the strongest part of the board, so landing there keeps it balanced and rolling straight.

check.q: Why does bending your knees on landing lower the force?
choices: It stops your motion over a longer time
It makes the board bounce higher
check.why: Stopping the same motion over a longer time needs less force.

check.q: In the worked example, stopping in 0.20 s instead of 0.05 s changes the force from 2,400 N to what?
check.why: 2.4 ÷ 0.20 = 12 m/s², and 50 × 12 = 600 N, one quarter of 2,400 N.

lessons.title: Standing Still on Grass
lessons.mainIdea: Practice the ollie standing still on grass or carpet, one step at a time, until the order of moves feels natural.
reading: Start with the board on grass or carpet and your helmet buckled. Stand in your ollie stance. First, practice only the pop: crouch, snap the tail and let the nose rise, without jumping. Do it ten times. Listen for the clack and feel the board bounce. This teaches your back foot the quick snap.

Next add the slide. Pop, then drag the front foot up toward the nose. Do not worry about height yet. Then add the jump and the knee lift. Finally add leveling and landing. This kind of *progression* lets your body learn each part before you put them together.

It helps to hold on at first. Rest one hand on a friend's shoulder or a sturdy fence at waist height. Learning the ollie usually takes many practice days. Short *sessions* of ten or fifteen minutes, done often, tend to work better than one long, tiring session.

Count your clean tries in a notebook. A clean try means all four wheels leave the ground and you land with both feet over the bolts. Watching the number grow shows real progress, even before the ollie looks high.

words.d: learning a skill in small steps, from the easiest part to harder ones
stretches of practice time, such as fifteen minutes on the grass

look.title: A Fifteen-Minute Grass Session
look.text: Minutes 1 to 3: stand on the board and rock gently to find your balance. Minutes 4 to 7: ten pops, no jump, listening for the clack. Minutes 8 to 11: ten pops with the front-foot slide, holding a friend's shoulder. Minutes 12 to 15: full ollies on the grass, counting each clean landing over the bolts.
look.prompt: Write your own fifteen-minute plan. Which step do you think you need the most time on, and why?

check.q: What should you practice first, standing still on grass?
check.why: Practicing only the pop teaches the back foot the quick snap before anything else is added.

check.q: Why build the ollie one step at a time?
choices: It keeps the grip tape new
Your body learns each part before you put them together
It is the only way to ride goofy
check.why: A progression adds one part at a time, so each part is learned before the whole trick.

check.q: Which practice plan tends to work better?
choices: Short sessions of 10 to 15 minutes, done often
Practicing only on days you feel perfect
check.why: Short, frequent sessions let you practice the timing often without getting worn out.

lessons.title: Rolling Ollies
lessons.mainIdea: Once the still ollie works, try it rolling slowly with your shoulders level and your weight centered.
reading: When you can ollie on grass and land over the bolts most of the time, move to smooth, flat pavement. Push once or twice and roll at about walking speed. Set your feet in ollie stance while rolling. Glance down once to check them, then look ahead.

A *rolling ollie* feels different at first. The board is moving under you, and fear can make you lean back. Leaning back sends the board out in front of you. Keep your shoulders over the bolts and your weight centered. Inertia carries you forward with the board, so you only need to jump up.

Start with tiny ollies, just a few centimeters high. Height comes later. When the rolling ollie feels steady, ollie over a chalk line, then a flat stick, then a folded towel. Each *obstacle* is a little higher than the last. A low, painted curb at a skatepark can come after that.

If you feel scared, that is a normal signal, and it is useful. Go back one step. Roll slower, or do a few more pops standing still. Confidence grows from many small successes. Writing down which step felt shaky shows you where to start next time.

words.d: an ollie done while the board is moving forward
something a skater ollies over or onto, such as a line, a stick or a low curb

look.title: A Ladder of Small Steps
look.text: Picture a ladder lying on the ground. The bottom rung is a still ollie on grass. The next rung is a rolling ollie at walking speed on pavement. Above that comes an ollie over a chalk line, then over a flat stick, then over a folded towel. The top rung is a low painted curb at a skatepark. You climb one rung at a time.
look.prompt: Which rung are you on now? What would show you that you are ready for the next one?

check.q: What happens if you lean back during a rolling ollie?
choices: The board shoots out in front of you
check.why: Leaning back pushes the board forward and away, so keep your shoulders over the bolts.

check.q: How fast should your first rolling ollies be?
choices: As fast as you can push
check.why: Rolling slowly makes it easier to stay balanced while you learn the timing.

check.q: Which is a good first object to ollie over?
choices: A chalk line on the ground
check.why: A chalk line has no height at all, so a mistake costs nothing. Higher objects come later, one small step at a time.

lessons.title: Fixing Common Problems
lessons.mainIdea: Most ollie problems come from the timing of the pop and slide or from where your weight sits, and each has a fix.
reading: Problem: the board barely leaves the ground. Fix: snap the tail faster and make sure the ball of your back foot hits the tail. Also check that you are jumping, not just pressing down. A light, quick pop beats a slow, heavy push.

Problem: the board shoots up and stands almost straight up on its tail, then falls back. Fix: slide your front foot farther toward the nose and push the nose down to level it. Problem: the board turns sideways in the air. Fix: point your shoulders along the board and snap the tail straight down, not off to one side.

Problem: your back foot stays heavy on the tail, so the tail drags. Fix: lift the back knee higher right after the pop. Problem: the board lands far in front of you. Fix: you jumped forward or leaned back, so jump straight up and keep your shoulders over the board. Good *timing*, each move at the right moment, solves most of these.

Filming your tries, in slow motion if you can, shows what your feet really do. Compare a good try and a bad try, then change one thing at a time so you know which fix worked. When a try goes wrong in the air, it is fine to *bail*: step off the board and land on your feet.

words.d: doing each move at the right moment and in the right order
to step or jump off the board on purpose when a trick goes wrong

look.title: Two Tries Side by Side
look.text: Try 1: the tail clacks, the front foot stays where it started, and the board stands up on its tail before slapping back down. Try 2: the tail clacks, the front shoe drags up to the nose, both knees lift, and the board flattens before landing under both feet. The only difference is what the front foot did after the pop.
look.prompt: Film two of your own tries. What is one difference you can see, and which fix will you try first?

check.q: The board shoots up and stands almost straight on its tail. What is the fix?
choices: Slide the front foot farther toward the nose and push it down to level
Move the back foot to the middle of the deck
check.why: A board that stands up means the front foot did not slide far enough or push the nose down.

check.q: The board turns sideways in the air. What should you check?
choices: That your shoulders point along the board and you snap straight down
check.why: Twisted shoulders or a sideways snap twist the board, so line the shoulders up and snap straight down.

check.q: A skater films an ollie try. What is the best way to use the video?
choices: Delete the bad tries without watching
Change every part of the ollie at once
Compare a good and a bad try, then change one thing at a time
check.why: Comparing tries shows the difference, and changing one thing at a time shows which fix worked.

review.q: Which list shows the steps of an ollie in order?
choices: Pop, slide, crouch, land, level, jump
Crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land
Slide, crouch, jump, pop, land, level
Jump, pop, crouch, level, slide, land
review.why: The ollie goes crouch, pop, slide, jump, level, land.

review.q: Where do the feet start for an ollie?
choices: Front foot on the nose, back foot over the back bolts
Back foot's ball on the tail, front foot just behind the front bolts
Front foot on the tail, back foot on the nose
review.why: The back foot pops the tail, and the front foot needs room behind the bolts to slide forward.

review.q: What makes the board rise when the tail strikes the ground?
choices: The ground pushes back up on the tail
review.why: By Newton's third law, the ground pushes back on the tail with an equal force, and the board pops up around the back wheels.

review.q: Why does an ollie need grip tape?
choices: Friction lets the front shoe drag the board upward
review.why: The rough tape creates friction, so the board follows the sliding front shoe up.

review.q: Who first did the ollie on flat ground, in the early 1980s?
review.why: Alan Gelfand's ollie was on ramps and bowls in the late 1970s. Rodney Mullen brought it to flat ground.

review.q: In the worked example, why is 600 N less than 2,400 N?
choices: The rider bent the knees and stopped over a longer time
review.why: Stopping in 0.20 s instead of 0.05 s cuts the deceleration, and so the force, to one quarter.

review.q: What is the best first place to practice the ollie?
choices: A sidewalk next to a busy street
Grass or carpet, where the wheels cannot roll
review.why: On grass or carpet the board stays under you while you learn the order of the moves.

review.q: You feel scared before a rolling ollie. What helps?
choices: Go back one step, such as rolling slower or popping standing still
Skate faster to get it over with
review.why: Fear is a normal signal. Breaking the trick into a smaller step builds confidence.

chapters.title: Shove-its, Kickflips and Heelflips
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a skater make a board spin or flip in the air and still land on it?

story.title: Wheels Down Again
story.kicker: A board spins under a jumping skater and lands wheels-down, and a friend asks how.
paragraphs: At the edge of the flat section, Ana popped and the board spun half a turn beneath her. It landed wheels-down, and she landed on it, rolling away with the old tail now in front. Her friend Marcus stopped pushing. He had seen the board turn, but Ana's body had not turned at all. How did the board come back around under her?

Ana stepped off and set the board on the grass beside the court. She showed him the back foot first. It did not just push down. It pushed down and swept backward, like scraping something off the ground behind her. The front foot barely did anything. It lifted out of the way and waited.

Then she showed him a different move, slowly, with no pop at all. Her front foot slid up the board and brushed off the edge of the nose. The board rolled over on the grass like a log, once, and came to rest grip tape up. That one, she said, is the start of a kickflip. The shove-it spins flat. The kickflip rolls.

Marcus held on to the fence and tried the flat spin on the grass. His first scoop sent the board barely a quarter turn. His second sent it all the way around and past. On the fifth try it stopped right at half a turn, nose and tail swapped. He looked up and grinned. Then he asked how long it takes to learn a kickflip.
story.think: How was the board's movement in Ana's shove-it different from its movement in her kickflip on the grass?

lessons.title: A Flat Spin Under Your Feet
lessons.mainIdea: In a pop shove-it, the board spins half a turn flat under you, around a vertical axis, while your body jumps straight up.
reading: Watch a *pop shove-it* from above. The skater pops, the board spins half a turn, and the nose and tail trade places. The skater lands on it again, now with the old tail in front. The board stays flat the whole time, grip tape up. It never flips over.

A half turn is 180 degrees, because a full circle is 360 degrees. The board turns around an *axis*, an imaginary line that something spins around. For a shove-it, the line goes straight up and down through the middle of the deck. This is the *vertical axis*. Picture a pencil stuck down through the center of the board, and the board turning around it like a spinning plate.

Your body does not spin with the board. You jump straight up and keep facing the same way, and only the board turns beneath you. So the trick needs two things: a pop to get the board off the ground, and a scoop to make it spin. A plain shove-it, with no pop, just spins the board flat along the ground.

words.d: a trick in which the skater pops the board and it spins 180 degrees flat beneath the skater
an imaginary line that an object turns around
a line running straight up and down through the middle of the deck; shove-its spin around it

look.title: How Far Shove-its Spin
look.cite: The number in each trick's name gives its spin; a full circle is 360 degrees
look.prompt: How many half turns does the board make in a 360 shove-it? In a 540 shove-it?

check.q: How far does the board spin in a pop shove-it?
check.why: A pop shove-it is a half turn, 180 degrees, so the nose and tail trade places.

check.q: Around which axis does the board spin in a shove-it?
choices: The long axis, from nose to tail
The axle of the back wheels
The short axis, across the deck
A vertical axis, straight up and down through the deck
check.why: The board stays flat and turns like a spinning plate, around a line straight up and down through its middle.

check.q: What does the skater's body do during a pop shove-it?
choices: Jumps straight up and keeps facing the same way
Spins 180 degrees along with the board
Leans far back over the tail
check.why: Only the board turns. The skater jumps straight up and lands facing the same direction.

lessons.title: The Scoop
lessons.mainIdea: For a backside pop shove-it, the back foot pops and scoops the tail behind you while the front foot lifts out of the way.
reading: Set your feet first. Put the ball of your back foot on the tail, near its toe-side edge. Your front foot rests lightly near the front bolts. The front foot does very little in this trick. It lifts away and then comes back down.

Now the motion. First crouch. Next, pop the tail down and at the same moment sweep it backward, behind you, toward your heel side. This sweeping push is the *scoop*. Your back foot moves as if it were scraping mud off the ground behind you. Then jump straight up and lift your front foot, so the board can spin freely beneath it.

This version is the *backside* pop shove-it, because the tail swings around behind your back. Most skaters learn it first. The *frontside* version scoops the tail forward, in front of your toes. Many skaters find the frontside spin harder to watch and catch. Both spin 180 degrees around the vertical axis.

The scoop gives the board a turning push. A push that makes something turn is a *torque*. The farther from the center of the turn the push lands, the more turning it gives. That is why the back foot scoops at the end of the tail, far from the middle of the deck.

words.d: the sweeping push of the back foot that makes the board spin in a shove-it
turning so the board or body swings around behind the skater's back
turning so the board or body swings around in front of the skater's toes
a turning push; torque equals force times the distance from the center of the turn

look.title: The Shove-it, Step by Step
look.text: Step 1: crouch, with the ball of the back foot near the toe-side edge of the tail. Step 2: pop and scoop the tail backward, behind you. Step 3: jump straight up and lift the front foot. Step 4: watch the board turn under you until the old tail is in front. Step 5: land with both feet over the bolts, knees bent.
look.prompt: On grass, do steps 1 and 2 with your front foot on the ground. How hard did you need to scoop to get exactly half a turn?

check.q: In a backside pop shove-it, which way does the back foot scoop the tail?
choices: Forward, in front of your toes
Backward, behind you toward your heel side
check.why: Backside means the tail swings around behind your back, so the back foot sweeps it backward.

check.q: What does the front foot do in a pop shove-it?
choices: Stays pressed down on the bolts
Lifts away so the board can spin, then comes back down
check.why: The back foot does the work. The front foot gets out of the way and lands again.

check.q: Why does the back foot scoop at the end of the tail?
choices: The tail is lighter than the rest of the board
The grip tape is rougher there
A push farther from the center gives more torque
check.why: Torque equals force times distance, so a push far from the middle gives more turning.

lessons.title: Practicing the Shove-it
lessons.mainIdea: Learn the shove-it on grass first, then rolling slowly, and fix problems one at a time.
reading: With your helmet buckled and pads on, start on grass or carpet. Practice the scoop alone, with your front foot on the ground beside the board. Scoop the tail and watch the board spin half a turn. Then step on with both feet over the bolts. This teaches the back foot how hard to scoop.

Next try the whole trick on the grass: crouch, pop and scoop, jump straight up, watch the board turn, and land on it. Then try it rolling slowly on smooth, flat ground. Keep your shoulders still and facing the same way. If your shoulders turn, your body follows the board and you land sideways.

Problem: the board spins too far, past 180 degrees. Fix: scoop more gently. Problem: the board turns only a quarter turn. Fix: scoop harder and farther behind you. Problem: the board lands behind you. Fix: you jumped backward, so jump straight up. Each try is *rotation* practice, learning how much push gives how much turn.

words.d: turning around an axis, measured in degrees
a turn of 90 degrees, one fourth of a full circle

look.title: Three Scoops on the Grass
look.text: Scoop 1 is soft, and the board turns about a quarter turn and stops sideways. Scoop 2 is hard, and the board turns all the way around and a bit past. Scoop 3 is in between, and the board stops with the nose and tail swapped, exactly half a turn. The skater's shoulders never move.
look.prompt: Try three scoops of different strengths on grass. Describe how far the board turned each time.

check.q: What is a good first step for learning the shove-it?
choices: Scoop the tail on grass with the front foot on the ground
Try it with your eyes closed
check.why: Scooping alone on grass teaches the back foot how hard to push before you jump.

check.q: The board spins past 180 degrees. What is the fix?
check.why: Too much scoop gives too much turn, so a softer scoop stops it at half a turn.

check.q: Why should you keep your shoulders still?
choices: So your body does not turn with the board and you land straight
check.why: If the shoulders turn, the body follows the board and you land sideways.

lessons.title: Kickflip Foot Position
lessons.mainIdea: For a kickflip, the back foot sits on the tail as for an ollie, and the front foot sits angled just behind the front bolts.
reading: A *kickflip* is an ollie in which the board also rolls over once in the air. Because it starts with the same pop, you need a steady ollie first. In the early 1980s Rodney Mullen worked out many tricks on flat ground, building on his flat-ground ollie, and flip tricks grew from that work. Today the kickflip is often the first flip trick skaters learn.

Back foot: the ball of the foot on the tail, as in an ollie. Some skaters move it a little toward the toe side. Front foot: just behind the front bolts, angled about 45 degrees so the toes point partly toward the nose. The foot sits near the middle of the board, not hanging off.

The angle matters because the front foot will slide up and off the nose's corner on the *toe side*, the long edge in front of your toes. A foot set straight across the board tends to make an ollie with no flip. A foot set too far back leaves no room to slide. Try a few spots on grass to find the one that feels natural.

words.d: an ollie in which the front foot flicks off the toe-side edge of the nose so the board rolls over once
the long edge of the board in front of the skater's toes
the long edge of the board behind the skater's heels

look.title: Ollie Feet and Kickflip Feet
look.text: Picture two boards side by side, seen from above. On the first, set for an ollie, the front foot lies straight across the board, a hand's width behind the front bolts. On the second, set for a kickflip, the front foot is turned about 45 degrees, toes aimed partly toward the nose. On both boards the back foot sits in the same place on the tail.
look.prompt: Stand in both stances on grass. How does turning the front foot change where it can slide?

check.q: What skill should you have before trying a kickflip?
check.why: The kickflip starts with the same pop as an ollie.

check.q: How is the front foot set for a kickflip?
choices: Angled about 45 degrees, just behind the front bolts
check.why: The angle lets the front foot slide up and off the toe-side corner of the nose.

check.q: What is the toe side of the board?
choices: The end behind the back bolts
The long edge in front of your toes
check.why: The toe side is the long edge in front of your toes; the heel side is the edge behind your heels.

lessons.title: The Flick
lessons.mainIdea: The front foot slides up and flicks off the toe-side corner of the nose, giving a torque that rolls the board around its long axis.
reading: First crouch. Next pop the tail exactly as in an ollie. Then slide your front foot up toward the nose, and near the top, *flick* it off the toe-side corner of the nose. The flick goes forward and out to the side, past the front of your toes. Then pull both knees up so the board can turn under you.

The flick pushes down on the very edge of the board. A deck is about 20 centimeters wide, so its edge is about 10 centimeters from the middle. A push there makes a torque around the board's *long axis*, the line from nose to tail. Torque = force × distance from the axis. A 20 N flick at 0.10 m gives 20 × 0.10 = 2 N·m. The same flick only 0.02 m from the middle gives 20 × 0.02 = 0.4 N·m, one fifth as much.

Why does the board roll over so easily? Most of its mass sits close to the long axis, because the deck is narrow. Mass close to an axis is easy to turn. Turning the board end over end would be much harder, because the nose and tail sit far from its middle.

A light flick is enough. Many learners kick too hard, and the board flips twice or flies away. Aim for one full roll, 360 degrees, while you are in the air. If the board keeps turning past one roll, the flick was too strong; if it stops halfway, it was too weak.

words.d: a quick brushing kick off the edge of the board that makes it flip
the line running from nose to tail through the middle of the board; kickflips and heelflips roll around it

look.title: Where the Flick Lands
look.cite: Worked example: a 20 N flick; torque = force × distance from the long axis
look.prompt: What would the torque be for the same 20 N flick at 0.06 m? Show the multiplication.

check.q: Where does the front foot flick in a kickflip?
choices: Off the heel-side edge of the tail
Off the toe-side corner of the nose
check.why: The front foot slides up and flicks off the toe-side corner of the nose.

check.q: A 20 N flick lands 0.10 m from the long axis. What is the torque?
check.why: Torque = force × distance = 20 × 0.10 = 2 N·m.

check.q: Why does the board roll easily around its long axis?
choices: Most of its mass is close to that line
check.why: The deck is narrow, so its mass sits close to the long axis, and mass near an axis is easy to turn.

lessons.title: Kickflip Problems and Fixes
lessons.mainIdea: Most kickflip problems come from flicking too hard or too soft, not jumping high enough, or leaning back.
reading: Problem: the board flips halfway and lands upside down. Fix: flick a little harder and farther out to the side, and pop higher so the board has more time. Problem: the board flips twice or shoots away. Fix: flick more softly, because the board needs only a light brush.

Problem: the board hits your *shins*. Fix: jump higher and pull your knees up sooner, and flick out to the side rather than straight forward. Some learners wear shin guards at this stage. Problem: the board lands far in front of you. Fix: you leaned back, so keep your shoulders over the board and jump straight up.

Problem: the board flips, but you are afraid to put your feet back on it. Fix: practice on grass, where the board cannot roll away. When you see the grip tape come around, step down with both feet over the bolts. If a try goes wrong, step off to the side and land on your feet, knees bent.

Flip tricks need *air time*. A 0.30 m ollie lasts about 0.49 seconds. To finish one 360 degree flip with time left to catch it, the board might turn in 0.30 s. That means 360 ÷ 0.30 = 1,200 degrees each second. A higher pop gives more time and makes the catch easier.

words.d: the fronts of the lower legs, below the knees
how long the skater and board stay off the ground during a trick

look.title: How Fast the Board Must Roll
look.cite: Worked example: one full flip of 360 degrees ÷ the time it takes
look.prompt: Which row leaves the most time to catch the board from a 0.49 second ollie? How much time is left?

check.q: The kickflip flips twice and shoots away. What is the fix?
choices: Move the back foot onto the nose
check.why: Two flips mean too much flick; the board needs only a light brush.

check.q: The board keeps hitting your shins. What helps?
choices: Jump higher and pull your knees up sooner
Flick straight down at the bolts
check.why: Lifting the knees sooner and higher gets your legs out of the board's path.

check.q: A board must turn 360 degrees in 0.30 seconds. How fast must it roll?
check.why: 360 ÷ 0.30 = 1,200 degrees per second.

lessons.title: Heelflip Foot Position
lessons.mainIdea: For a heelflip, the front foot points across the board with the toes slightly over the toe-side edge, so the heel can reach the other edge.
reading: A *heelflip* is the kickflip's partner. The board also rolls once around its long axis. This time the front heel does the flick instead of the side of the foot. Because the push lands on the opposite edge, the board rolls in the opposite direction from a kickflip.

Back foot: the ball of the foot on the tail, as in an ollie. Front foot: just behind the front bolts, pointing straight across the board. Let the toes hang slightly over the toe-side edge. In this spot, the heel sits near the heel-side edge, where it can catch the corner of the nose.

Check the stance on grass before you pop. Slide your front foot forward and swing your heel out over the heel side. If your heel cannot reach past the edge, move the foot slightly toward the toe side. The stance should feel balanced and steady, not tippy.

words.d: an ollie in which the front heel flicks off the heel-side edge of the nose so the board rolls over once
the reverse way; a heelflip rolls the reverse way from a kickflip

look.title: Kickflip Feet and Heelflip Feet
look.text: Picture the front foot from above on two boards. For the kickflip, the foot is angled about 45 degrees, ready to slide off the toe-side corner of the nose. For the heelflip, the foot points straight across the board, toes just over the toe-side edge and heel near the heel-side edge. The back foot is the same on both.
look.prompt: Set up both stances on grass. Which edge of the board is your heel closest to in the heelflip stance?

check.q: Which part of the foot flicks the board in a heelflip?
choices: The side of the front foot
check.why: In a heelflip the front heel does the flick, off the heel-side edge of the nose.

check.q: Where do the front toes go for a heelflip?
choices: Hanging slightly over the toe-side edge
check.why: With the toes just over the toe-side edge, the heel sits near the heel-side edge, ready to flick.

check.q: How does a heelflip's roll compare with a kickflip's?
choices: It spins flat like a shove-it
It rolls in the opposite direction
check.why: The heel pushes the opposite edge, so the board rolls the opposite way around the same long axis.

lessons.title: The Heel Flick
lessons.mainIdea: Pop, then kick the front heel forward and out off the heel-side corner of the nose, and let the board roll.
reading: First crouch. Next pop the tail as in an ollie. Then slide your front foot up and kick your heel forward and out, so it brushes off the heel-side corner of the nose. The kick goes away from your toes, out over the heel side. Then lift both knees so the board can roll beneath you.

Compare the two flicks. In a kickflip, the push goes down on the toe-side *edge*. In a heelflip, the push goes down on the heel-side edge. Each push makes a torque around the long axis. Because the pushes land on opposite edges, the torques turn opposite ways, and so does the board.

Problem: the board shoots forward. Fix: kick more out to the side than forward. Problem: the board turns sideways while it flips. Fix: keep your shoulders lined up with the board. Problem: the board only half flips. Fix: get your heel all the way to the edge before you kick. Every *flip trick* rewards a steady pop first.

words.d: one of the two long sides of the deck: the toe-side edge or the heel-side edge
a trick in which the board rolls or spins under the skater's feet in the air

look.title: Two Flicks, Two Directions
look.text: Hold a skateboard in front of you by its nose and tail, grip tape up. Press down on the edge nearest you and the board rolls one way. Press down on the far edge and it rolls the other way. The kickflip presses one long edge and the heelflip presses the other, so the board rolls in opposite directions.
look.prompt: Try this with a board held off the ground. Which edge did you press to copy a heelflip, the toe-side edge or the heel-side edge?

check.q: In a heelflip, which way does the heel kick?
choices: Forward and out over the heel side
Up into the air without touching the board
check.why: The heel brushes off the heel-side corner of the nose, kicking forward and out.

check.q: Why do a kickflip and a heelflip roll in opposite directions?
choices: One is done regular and the other goofy
The pushes land on opposite edges, so the torques turn opposite ways
Kickflips do not use the long axis
check.why: The kickflip pushes the toe-side edge and the heelflip pushes the heel-side edge.

check.q: The heelflip board shoots forward. What is the fix?
choices: Kick more out to the side than forward
Move the back foot onto the nose
check.why: A kick aimed too far forward pushes the board ahead, so aim it out to the side.

lessons.title: Telling Flips Apart
lessons.mainIdea: Flip tricks are named by which part of the foot flicks and which edge gets the push, and they can be mixed with shove-it spins.
reading: Skaters name flip tricks by what the front foot does. A kickflip uses the side of the front foot and the toe-side edge. A heelflip uses the heel and the heel-side edge. Both start with an ollie pop, and both roll the board 360 degrees around the long axis.

Many skaters find one of the two easier. Neither is more correct, and learning both gives you control in both directions. Watching a friend from the front shows the difference. In a kickflip, the edge nearest the toes dips first. In a heelflip, the edge nearest the heels dips first.

Flips can be mixed with spins. A *varial kickflip* adds a pop shove-it's 180 degree spin to a kickflip. A *360 flip*, also called a tre flip, adds a full 360 degree shove-it spin to a kickflip. These tricks turn the board around the long axis and the vertical axis at once. Skaters usually learn them only after the single tricks feel steady.

words.d: a kickflip combined with the 180 degree flat spin of a pop shove-it
a kickflip combined with a full 360 degree shove-it spin; also called a tre flip

look.title: Watching From the Front
look.text: Stand in front of a friend who is doing slow flicks on grass. On one try, the edge nearest their toes dips and the board rolls toward you. On the next, their heel kicks out behind them, the far edge dips, and the board rolls the other way. Same board, same long axis, opposite rolls.
look.prompt: Watch two slow flicks on grass. Name each one as a kickflip or a heelflip, and say which clue told you.

check.q: Which edge gets the push in a kickflip?
check.why: The side of the front foot flicks down on the toe-side edge.

check.q: What is a varial kickflip?
choices: A kickflip combined with a pop shove-it's 180 degree spin
A kickflip done on a rail
check.why: A varial kickflip mixes a kickflip's roll with a pop shove-it's half-turn spin.

check.q: A 360 flip combines a kickflip with what?
check.why: The 360 flip, or tre flip, adds a full 360 degree shove-it spin to a kickflip.

lessons.title: The Three Axes of a Board
lessons.mainIdea: Every board trick turns around one or more of three axes: the long axis, the short axis and the vertical axis.
reading: Picture three sticks pushed through the center of a skateboard. One runs from nose to tail: the long axis. One runs across the deck from the toe-side edge to the heel-side edge: the *short axis*. One runs straight up and down through the deck: the vertical axis. Every turn a board makes in the air happens around one of these lines, or more than one at once.

Each trick family uses a different axis. Kickflips and heelflips roll the board around the long axis. Shove-its spin it around the vertical axis. The ollie's nose-up tilt is a small turn around the short axis. A *combination trick* such as the 360 flip uses two axes at the same time.

The axes also explain how hard a turn is. A board is about 80 centimeters long and about 20 centimeters wide. Around the long axis, all of its mass sits within about 10 centimeters, so it rolls easily. Around the short and vertical axes, the nose and tail are about 40 centimeters away, so the board resists turning more. Scientists call this resistance *rotational inertia*.

words.d: the line running across the deck from the toe-side edge to the heel-side edge
a trick that mixes two moves, such as a flip and a spin, at the same time
how strongly an object resists being turned; it is larger when mass sits far from the axis

look.title: Three Pencils Through a Board
look.text: Imagine a small model board with three pencils stuck through its center. The first pencil points from nose to tail. The second points across, from edge to edge. The third points straight up. Twirl the model around each pencil in turn. Around the first, it rolls like a log. Around the second, it turns end over end. Around the third, it spins flat like a plate.
look.prompt: Name the pencil, or axis, for each of these: kickflip, pop shove-it, heelflip.

check.q: A heelflip rolls the board around which axis?
check.why: Kickflips and heelflips both roll the board around the long axis, from nose to tail.

check.q: A pop shove-it spins the board around which axis?
check.why: A shove-it spins flat, around a line straight up and down through the deck.

check.q: Why is the board harder to spin around the vertical axis than to roll around the long axis?
choices: Its nose and tail are far from that axis, so its rotational inertia is larger
It is lighter when it spins flat
Gravity pulls only on the nose
check.why: Mass far from an axis resists turning more, and the nose and tail are about 40 cm from the vertical axis.

lessons.title: Catching the Board
lessons.mainIdea: Catching means stopping the board's turn with your feet as the grip tape comes back up, then landing over the bolts.
reading: A flip trick is finished only when you catch it. To *catch* means to stop the board's turning with your feet and land on it. Watch the board the whole time it is in the air. When the grip tape comes back up under you, that is the moment to put your feet down.

In a kickflip, many skaters catch with the back foot first. The back foot comes down on the tail and stops the roll. The front foot then lands over the front bolts. In a pop shove-it, both feet usually come down together once the board has turned 180 degrees. Either way, aim for both feet over the bolts with your knees bent.

Stopping a turn takes a torque in the opposite direction, and your feet supply it. When your shoe presses on the turning board, the push of your foot and the grip of the tape slow the turn. A firm, flat foot stops the turn cleanly. A foot that lands on the *edge* of a still-turning board can tip it and roll your ankle.

After the catch, bend your knees, stay low and roll away. Rolling away steady is part of landing the trick. Keep your shoulders over the board while you roll, because leaning back sends it out in front of you. If the board wobbles, look ahead and let your bent knees soak up the bumps.

words.d: to stop a turning board with your feet and land on it
one of the long sides of the deck, where a foot can tip the board if it lands there

look.title: Watching for the Grip Tape
look.text: A kickflip from the skater's eyes: the board leaves the ground and turns over, showing the dark wheels and trucks for a blink. Then a strip of black grip tape swings back into view. That is the cue. The back foot drops onto the tail, the roll stops, and the front foot comes down over the front bolts.
look.prompt: On grass, flick the board without jumping and say 'now' when you see the grip tape come back up. How quickly does it happen?

check.q: What does it mean to catch a flip trick?
choices: To grab the board with your hands
To stop the board's turning with your feet and land on it
To pick up the board after a fall
check.why: Catching uses the feet to stop the board's turn so you can land on it.

check.q: When should you put your feet down on a flipping board?
choices: When the wheels face the sky
When the grip tape comes back up under you
Only after the board hits the ground
check.why: The grip tape coming back up shows the board has finished its turn and is ready to stand on.

check.q: Why should your foot land flat over the bolts, not on an edge?
choices: It makes the board flip again
A foot on an edge can tip the board and roll your ankle
check.why: A firm, flat foot over the bolts stops the turn cleanly; landing on an edge can tip the board.

lessons.title: Practicing Flips Slowly
lessons.mainIdea: Practice flip motions slowly and in parts, on grass and holding a support, before trying them rolling.
reading: Practice the flick standing still on grass or carpet, with your helmet buckled and wrist guards on. Hold a friend's shoulder or a sturdy fence. Without popping, slide your front foot up and flick off the nose. Watch how the board rolls. Keep going until the flick sends the board around once, not twice and not halfway.

Next add a small pop while still holding on. Then let go and try the whole trick on the grass. Try it rolling slowly on smooth, flat ground only after you can catch it on grass several times in a row. Each step gets you ready for the next.

Slow practice helps because your brain learns a movement as a pattern. Repeating the right pattern many times makes it *automatic*, so it happens without thinking during the fast real trick. People often call this *muscle memory*, though the learning really happens in the brain. Rushing to full speed too soon can build a habit of the wrong motion.
Rest matters too. Flip practice is hard on ankles and shins. Stop when you feel tired, because tired legs pop lower and land less steadily. Ending on a good try helps you remember how it felt.

words.d: done without having to think about each step
the everyday name for a movement that has become automatic through practice; the learning happens in the brain

look.title: Four Sessions Toward a Kickflip
look.text: Session 1: flicks on grass without popping, holding a fence, until the board rolls once. Session 2: small pops with the flick, still holding on. Session 3: the whole kickflip on grass without holding on, catching with the back foot first. Session 4: if catches on grass come several times in a row, slow rolling tries on smooth, flat ground.
look.prompt: Which session sounds hardest to you? What could you add between two sessions to make the jump smaller?

check.q: What should you practice first for a kickflip?
choices: The flick, standing still on grass while holding a support
check.why: The flick alone, on grass and holding on, is the smallest first step.

check.q: When is it time to try a flip trick while rolling?
choices: After your first try on grass
After you can catch it on grass several times in a row
Before you try it on grass
check.why: Steady catches on grass show the pattern is ready for a moving board.

check.q: Why does slow, repeated practice help?
choices: It wears in the grip tape
check.why: Repeating the right pattern makes it automatic, so it happens during the fast real trick.

review.q: How do a pop shove-it and a kickflip differ?
choices: The shove-it spins flat around the vertical axis; the kickflip rolls around the long axis
The kickflip spins flat; the shove-it rolls over
review.why: The shove-it turns like a spinning plate; the kickflip rolls over like a log.

review.q: In a backside pop shove-it, what does the back foot do?
choices: Pops and scoops the tail behind you
review.why: The back foot pops the tail and sweeps it backward, behind your back.

review.q: In a kickflip, the front foot flicks off which part of the board?
choices: The heel-side edge of the tail
The toe-side corner of the nose
review.why: The side of the front foot slides up and flicks off the toe-side corner of the nose.

review.q: What does the heel do in a heelflip?
choices: Kicks off the heel-side corner of the nose
review.why: The front heel brushes forward and out off the heel-side corner of the nose.

review.q: A 25 N flick lands 0.08 m from the long axis. What is the torque?
Which axis does the ollie's nose-up tilt turn around?
choices: The wheel axle of the front truck
review.why: The nose rising and tail dropping is a turn around the short axis, across the deck.

review.q: What is the cue to catch a kickflip?
choices: The grip tape coming back up under you
review.why: When the grip tape comes back up, the board has finished its roll and is ready to land on.

review.q: Why does a higher pop make flip tricks easier?
choices: It gives more air time to finish the flip and catch it
It stops the board from turning
review.why: A higher ollie stays in the air longer, so the board has time to turn and you have time to catch it.
